title: The audit problem: Scattered logs and unverifiable claims
text: This is Onyx in for Humanitarian's AI. This week on the Microft Finance Investigator, the audit question. The investigator now has validated data, deterministic math, adversarial evaluations, scenario analysis, and an open review gate, but that evidence is scattered across dozens of files. So this week, can you package it into one bundle that proves every artifact came from the same investigation and let a reviewer check it independently? Act one, the scattered proof. Each week added a real capability, and each one wrote its own files, logs, results, reports, hashes. Individually, they're trustworthy, but a reviewer shouldn't have to take it on faith that this evaluation, that scenario, and this review request all describe the same run. Belonging has to be provable, not

title: Establishing the 7 distinct links that must hash-match before bundling
text: Assumed. Act two, validate then package. Before it packages anything, the bundle rederives the links. The review request has to carry the same run ID in the same SHA-256 as the investigation log. The scenario output has to hash match that baseline run and its plan. If any link is broken, packaging stops with an error. You cannot bundle evidence that doesn't provably belong together. Seven things have to line up before a single file is copied. The investigation run ID, the validation result, the review request hash, the evaluation case hash, the scenario plan hash, the raw data hashes, and the verified data hashes. Miss one and nothing gets packaged. Only then

title: Packaging 54 artifacts with an integrity manifest and review.md
text: Does it package 54 artifacts in one folder. Raw and verified finance data, configuration schemas, the implementation code, the tests, the investigation and evaluation and scenario logs, the human-readable reports, the recipe, and the conductor. Alongside them, three integrity files, a manifest of every hash, a checksum of that manifest, and a human-readable review.md. Act three, verify independently. There's a separate command for the reviewer, verify bundle. It rereads the manifest and review checksums, recomputes the size and SHA-256 of every packaged artifact, and rejects any file that's extra, missing, or altered. When everything lines up, it prints one status, integrity matched,

title: Rerunning verification independently and catching 7 tamper cases
text: Human review open. And it's proven by trying to break it. Seven tamper cases each rejected, an altered manifest, a modified reviewer view, a changed packaged artifact, an extra unlisted file, a mismatched run hash, an unsafe bundle name, and an overwrite attempt. Nine bundle tests in all, bringing the project to 41 passing and both GitHub CI checks green. But be precise about what this proves. SHA-256 checks improves file integrity, that these exact bytes have not changed since packaging. It does not prove identity. It does not prove the work is adequate, and it is not a human approval. The bundle even says so in its own words. So, the bundle ships nothing. The recipe stays labeled draft. The release status is blocked pending human review, and

title: What SHA-256 proves (integrity) vs. what it doesn't (adequacy & approval)
text: Five gates stay visibly open, materiality approval, and evidence-backed causal explanation, evaluation adequacy, scenario approval, and distribution authorization. The machine packaged the proof. A named human still has to decide. The verdict this week turned scattered evidence into an audible package. The bundle validates the whole chain by hash, run, review, evaluation, scenario, and both raw and verified data, before packaging 54 artifacts with a manifest, a checksum, and a review file. An independent verify bundle recomputes everything and reports integrity matched, human review open, with seven tamper cases rejected. SHA-256 proves integrity, not identity, adequacy, or approval. So, the recipe stays draft, the release stays blocked, and five human gates stay open.

title: Keeping the recipe as draft and human verification gates open
text: Your turn. An answer you can't reproduce isn't evidence, it's just a claim. So, think about the tools you rely on and answer in the comments. If an agent gives you an answer, but cannot prove exactly which data, code, tests, and decisions produced it, can you really audit it? Can you prove what your finance agent actually did? This is Onyx in for Humanitarian's AI.
